title: KV-cache eviction / paging / prefix-reuse deep dive with Cobalt Systems
summary: Deep technical troubleshooting session on KV cache evictions, paging behavior under long-context sessions, and prefix reuse patterns. Redwood SE walked through cache internals, heuristics for eviction, metrics to surface, and mitigations (sharding, pinning, aggressive prefetch, tuning batch/window sizes). Customer shared reproduction of evictions during long chat sessions and intermittent latency spikes on Dedicated. Action items include running benchmark harness, sharing eviction metrics, and testing a pinned-prefix config in a staging pod.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Patel: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. We are here to run a deep dive into the KV-cache behavior you saw on Dedicated. um Jonah and Lina from our infra team are here. Arjun, do you want to kick off with the customer reproduction?
[00:00:18] Arjun Rao: Yeah thanks Maya. So we run a long-chat workflow — user sessions that go 8k to 20k tokens — and after a while we start seeing a lot of soft evictions, and then throughput drops and latency spikes. It's most visible when multiple users have overlapping prefixes.
[00:00:35] Sara Mills: To add, evictions show up as a huge uptick in token compute because KV misses force recompute and we see p99 go from ~180ms to 450-600ms.
[00:00:45] Jonah Kim (Redwood SE): Okay that tracks with what we'd expect when the KV working set exceeds available memory. Quick clarifying q: are you seeing physical OOMs or just evictions?
[00:00:54] Diego Fernandes: No OOMs, just eviction churn and paging; disk I/O also increases a bit. We're on Dedicated with 2x A100 pods, 256GB RAM per node, and we run 4 model shards.
[00:01:07] Lina Herrera: Thanks. Two causes commonly: either the per-shard KV size grows due to long contexts and prefix reuse leads to duplicated entries, or the eviction heuristics are too blunt for your access patterns.
[00:01:19] Priya Nair: We suspect prefix reuse is the big one — lots of similar system prompts and user intents rerun across sessions. Could be duplication.
[00:01:26] Jonah: Right, prefix reuse is a sneaky multiplier. If different sessions produce slightly different tokenization offsets or different user IDs in metadata, the cache keys diverge. That creates many cold entries that look similar but are distinct, so working set balloons.
[00:01:40] Arjun: Is there a difference in how Redwood handles exact-match vs prefix-match keys?
[00:01:45] Jonah: We hash a {model, shard, sequence-offset, kv-prefix-hash} tuple. If any minor change in prompt text or in tokenization occurs, it's a different key. We've seen customers consolidate keys by normalizing system prompt tokens or by pinning core prefixes.
[00:01:58] Sara: When you say pinning, do you mean permanent resident cache entries? How does that impact memory?
[00:02:05] Lina: Pinning keeps the prefix in memory and prevents eviction for that entry. It's great for hot prefixes but increases resident working set. So you have to be judicious — pin only top-k prefixes by frequency.
[00:02:17] Diego: We tried a naive pin of the top 50 prefixes and p99 improved but then overall memory usage still climbed until we hit eviction thresholds on other prefixes.
[00:02:29] Jonah: That's expected. We recommend a tiered approach: pinned top N, a probabilistic LRU for warm entries, and a cold bucket that allows prefetch into an SSD-backed page store. That reduces eviction recoils.
[00:02:42] Arjun: SSD-backed page store — do you mean Redwood supports paging KV pages to local NVMe?
[00:02:47] Maya: Short answer yes in Dedicated/private — we have an optional persistent page store that moves cold KV pages to local NVMe and rehydrates on demand. But there is a latency cost for misses.
[00:02:59] Priya: Related — Diego mentioned disk I/O rising. Is it possible that our paging threshold is too low so we thrash between mem and NVMe?
[00:03:06] Jonah: Absolutely. Thrashing happens if the hot working set is near the memory threshold and the eviction/prefetch windows are too small. Two knobs: increase in-memory quota, or increase hysteresis before demoting to SSD. Also adjust prefetch size so rehydration is amortized.
[00:03:23] Sara: Any guidance on sizing for 20k token sessions? We run a lot of multi-turn with embeddings and retrieval augmentation.
[00:03:30] Lina: For long-context you should plan KV size per session ~ O(sequence_length * model_kv_size). For a 20k token session on a 1.5B KV-per-token assumption that's roughly X GB per session — sorry that's hand-wavy — we can send a calculator. Key is concurrency: if you have 100 active long sessions concurrently, multiply accordingly.
[00:03:49] Arjun: We hit the sweet spot where 20 concurrent long sessions pushes us into eviction land.
[00:03:54] Jonah: So routes forward: 1) reduce duplicates with prefix normalization, 2) shard differently to balance hot prefixes, 3) pin hottest prefixes, 4) increase memory or add NVMe fast page store, 5) tune batch/window sizes to reduce KV churn.
[00:04:08] Diego: On #2 sharding — we currently use static hash-based sharding by conversation ID. Could rebalancing by prefix-hotness help?
[00:04:16] Jonah: Yes dynamic shard placement or hotspot-aware routing helps. Hot prefixes concentrated on one shard cause localized pressure. We can route requests with hot prefixes to dedicated shards or replicate hot prefixes on read-only shards to avoid cross-shard eviction storms.
[00:04:31] Priya: How complex is replication? Storage overhead is high but we may accept it for very hot system prompts.
[00:04:37] Lina: We support configurable replication factors at the prefix granularity in Dedicated — again trade memory for latency stability.
[00:04:45] Arjun: You mentioned batches — we use a 16-token batching window for throughput. Any interaction with KV behavior?
[00:04:51] Jonah: Batching impacts cache hit patterns. Larger batches increase simultaneous KV lookups which can amplify misses; but batching also amortizes kernel launch overhead. If misses are the main issue, smaller batch windows or prioritized caching for expected prefixes helps.
[00:05:06] Sara: Quantization — could switching quantization profiles reduce KV size? We saw model artifacts change with 4-bit configs.
[00:05:12] Lina: Quantization primarily affects model weights memory, not KV cache storage, except if model changes tokenization slightly or alters attention behavior leading to different KV lifetimes. The main memory win isn't in KV but in host/GPU memory used by the model.
[00:05:25] Arjun: Ok fair. On the monitoring side, we don't have fine-grained metrics for per-prefix eviction rates; we only see per-shard evictions.
[00:05:33] Jonah: You should instrument top-k prefix counters and eviction latencies. We recommend export of: per-prefix hit-rate, eviction count, rehydrate latency, and page-store IO ops. Also trace token-level spikes to correlate to specific prefixes.
[00:05:47] Diego: Is there an existing dashboard template in Console?
[00:05:50] Maya: Yes, we'll share a dashboard template. Action item: Jonah will drop a Grafana JSON with the KV panels.
[00:05:58] Priya: A specific thing we observed: after a model rollback to an earlier variant, eviction spiked immediately. Is that expected?
[00:06:05] Lina: If the model variant changes tokenizer or adds metadata in prompts, keys diverge and you lose reuse — yes you'll see a spike. Sometimes fallback policies can map older keys to new ones but that's brittle.
[00:06:17] Arjun: Let's talk about prefix normalization in practice. We have variable user IDs and timestamps in system prompts — can Redwood strip or canonicalize those?
[00:06:25] Jonah: Yes, we have a small preprocessor hook in the serving path where you can define normalization rules: strip user-id tokens, remove ephemeral timestamps, canonicalize email tokens. That reduces key cardinality significantly.
[00:06:39] Sara: Any cost to preprocessing?
[00:06:41] Jonah: Very small CPU cost — typically <1-2ms per request. Worth it if it reduces KV working set by 10-100x.
[00:06:50] Diego: On VPC/on-prem we have kernel limits and mmap/uLimits. Could those cause unexpected eviction behavior?
[00:06:57] Lina: System-level limits like overcommitted mem, file descriptor limits, and cgroup memory throttling can cause eviction thrash if not tuned. On-prem kernels with transparent hugepages also change memory footprint. We have a tuning doc we'll share.
[00:07:09] Priya: Good. Another signal: we saw eviction correlating with large batch writes from other tenants on the same host — noisy neighbor.
[00:07:16] Jonah: Right that's where Dedicated isolation matters; if you are on shared hardware, you can get cross-tenant pressure. For Dedicated we enforce quotas and can reserve memory pools per tenant.
[00:07:27] Arjun: Any quick wins we can try this week?
[00:07:30] Maya: Yes, Jonah?
[00:07:31] Jonah: Quick wins: 1) enable prefix normalization rules for top 20 prefixes, 2) decrease batch window from 16 to 12 for a test cohort, 3) pin top 10 prefixes only, 4) increase page-store hysteresis threshold. We can push a staging config.
[00:07:46] Priya: We'll try that on staging. How do we measure success?
[00:07:49] Lina: Look for reduction in per-shard eviction rate, lower p99 latency, and lower NVMe read ops. We'll give baseline queries to run.
[00:07:58] Diego: Security/compliance note — when we talk about pinning and replication, does that increase data retention concerns? Some prefixes can contain PII.
[00:08:06] Maya: Good call. For any pinned or replicated data you can enable encryption-at-rest with customer KMS and set retention TTLs. We'll share the compliance docs.
[00:08:15] Arjun: Last — timeline. We want to run a 2-week pilot with a staging cluster and then a production pilot. Is that feasible?
[00:08:22] Maya: Yes. We'll scope a pilot.
[00:08:26] Priya: Sweet. Thanks all.
[00:08:29] Maya: Quick recap and next steps coming from me.
[00:08:32] [intermittent crosstalk — audio drop ~1s]
[00:08:40] Maya: Okay, end of meeting notes.
[00:08:43] 
[00:30:00] [long chunk omitted — detailed whiteboard session on sharding algorithm and pseudo configs; participants annotated graphs]
[00:45:12] Jonah: Summarizing the config snippet: shard-hotness routing policy, pinned-prefix list (sha256 ids), page-store threshold at 75% mem with hysteresis 10%, prefetch size 4MB, replication factor 2 for top prefixes.
[00:46:20] Sara: We'll try the pinned-prefix list and route the hot prefixes to a replica shard.
[00:46:40] Lina: We'll also send a micro-benchmark harness — runs synthetic long-context patterns and emits per-prefix metrics.
[00:47:00] Arjun: We'll instrument and share the logs.
[00:47:10] Maya: Great. Anything else?
[00:47:14] Priya: One ask — can Redwood provide an example normalizer regex pack for common system prompts?
[00:47:20] Jonah: Yes we'll include.
[00:47:25] Diego: Thanks all.
[00:47:28] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the deck, dashboard JSON, and pilot proposal.
